title: Loneliness Biases Social Engagement Decisions: Evidence From Value‐Based Choice Models
content:
In two preregistered studies, participants first completed an expectation priming task (positive, neutral, or negative) and subsequently made decisions in a vignette-based social decision task in which potential reward, required effort, and social threat were systematically manipulated. Exploratory analyses indicated that higher loneliness was associated with attenuated sensitivity to both rewarding and threatening social cues. Furthermore, loneliness was linked to diminished differentiation between high- and low-reward contexts, reflecting a narrowed range of subjective social value across decision scenarios.


ABSTRACT

Loneliness is a well-established risk factor for adverse mental health outcomes and persistent social withdrawal. We tested whether loneliness is associated with systematic alterations in value-based social decision-making and examined mechanisms that may sustain withdrawal. Across two preregistered online studies (total N = 6517), participants were randomly assigned to positive, negative, or neutral social expectation priming and completed a vignette-based task manipulating reward, effort, and threat. Loneliness and psychopathological symptoms were assessed by self-reports. Across both studies, higher loneliness was consistently associated with a lower likelihood of engaging in social interactions, independent of vignette characteristics and expectation priming. Higher loneliness was consistently associated with lower anticipated connectedness and greater perceived rejection risk during social decision-making. Further exploratory analyses indicated that loneliness was associated with reduced sensitivity to both social reward and social threat, accompanied by diminished differentiation between high- and low-reward contexts, consistent with a compressed range of subjective social value across decision scenarios. These findings suggest that loneliness is linked to altered social valuation, characterized by blunted differentiation of social rewards and reduced motivational salience of potentially beneficial interactions, contributing to persistent withdrawal across diverse everyday social contexts.
